question: The _post hoc_ fallacy is

arguing that a single event caused another when the cause is really several events
drawing a conclusion about a causal relationship based on hearsay or anecdotal evidence
arguing that since two events are unrelated, one cannot have caused the other
model_outputs:
We refer to Wikipedia articles on logic and fallacies for help. The *post hoc ergo propter hoc* fallacy is a specific type of causal fallacy where one assumes that because event B occurred after event A, event A must have caused event B.

Reviewing the options:
A. arguing that since one event preceded another event the first event must have caused the second event (This perfectly describes the core of the *post hoc* fallacy.)
B. drawing a conclusion about a causal relationship when there is no evidence of a causal relationship (This is a broader definition of a causal fallacy, but less specific to *post hoc*.)
C. arguing that since two things happened at the same time one must have caused the other (This describes *simultaneity* fallacy or confusing correlation with causation.)
D. arguing that a single event caused another when there is no logical connection between them (This describes a general causal fallacy.)
E. drawing a conclusion about a causal relationship based on a single instance (This is often related to hasty generalization.)
F. arguing that an event must have caused another because they are correlated (This is correlation vs. causation.)
G. arguing that a single event caused another when the cause is really several events (This is a specific nuance of causal error, but not the primary definition of *post hoc*.)
H. drawing a conclusion about a causal relationship based on hearsay or anecdotal evidence (This describes the appeal to anecdote.)
I. arguing that since two events are unrelated, one cannot have caused the other (This is the fallacy of false dichotomy/non sequitur.)

Option A is the most precise definition of the *post hoc* fallacy.

the answer is (A)
